items.title: Thelma Golden To Step Down From Role as Director of Studio Museum in Harlem
items.summary:
Thelma Golden, the director and chief curator of the Studio Museum in Harlem, will step down from her position in late 2027, the museum announced Tuesday.

The announcement coincides with Golden’s 20th anniversary in the role, which she assumed in 2006, and comes just one year after the museum reopened in a new, purpose-built building after a seven-year closure. The new $125 million building was designed by architect David Adjaye and provides 82,000 square feet across seven floors, including a 139-seat public lobby, a rooftop terrace, education spaces, a library, and a cafe. It received rave reviews upon its reopening.

Kathryn C. Chenault, chair of the museum’s board of trustees, said in a statement that the board has formed a search committee to identify Golden’s successor and has retained an international executive search firm to assist. Golden will remain in her post until a replacement is hired.

While Golden’s departure was not entirely expected, it is not unusual for museum directors to exit their positions after a major renovation or expansion. Lisa Phillips announced in September 2025 that she would leave her role as director of the New Museum after its reopening, and Janne Sirén, director of the Buffalo AKG Art Museum, said in April that he would step down following the museum’s 2023 expansion.

“I know this is the right moment to begin this transition—and as I look ahead to new projects and opportunities, I also look back with gratitude toward the many people whose achievements have been my bedrock,” Golden said in a statement. “I think of my teachers, mentors,…
items.t: Thelma Golden To Step Down From Role as Director of Studio Museum in Harlem

items.title: Military History Museum in Dresden Agrees to Return Contested Nazi-Era Family Archive to Jehovah’s Witnesses
items.summary:
Five years after the Jehovah’s Witnesses sued the German government over ownership of an archive tracing one family’s persecution by the Nazi regime, the files have been returned to the religious organization, reports the New York Times . Jehovah’s Witnesses were targeted by the Nazis specifically for their refusal to salute Hitler, display the swastika flag, or serve in the military; 4,500 were sent to concentration camps, and 1,800 died during the Nazi era.

The more than 1,000 documents, photographs, drawings, letters, and reports that make up the archive were collected and saved for decades by Annemarie Kusserow, one of 11 children from a Jehovah’s Witness family that lived in the town of Bad Lippspringe in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. According to an oral history published by the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum, the Kusserow home was searched by the Gestapo 20 times, and the Kusserow parents, Hilda and Franz, were the first to be arrested, in the mid-1930s. The children eventually ended up in prisons, concentration camps, or training schools. Two brothers, Wilhelm and Wolfgang, were murdered by the Nazis, and another survived the war but died shortly after from tuberculosis contracted at Dachau.

At the time of her death in 2005, Annemarie Kusserow’s will stated that her family’s archive should go to the Jehovah’s Witnesses. But one of her brothers, Hans Werner Kusserow, had the archive in his possession at the time, and in 2009 he sold it to the Bundeswehr Military History Museum in Dresden. This was “especially troubling,” the Jehovah’s Witnesses’ official…
items.t: Military History Museum in Dresden Agrees to Return Contested Nazi-Era Family Archive to Jehovah’s Witnesses

items.title: Bukhara Biennial Unveils ‘The Long Welcome’ Theme and Names First Artists
items.summary:
After an inaugural edition last year, the Bukhara Biennial will return to Uzbekistan in 2027, this time with “The Long Welcome” as a theme (after 2025’s theme of “Recipes for Broken Hearts”). As announced this past summer, the artistic director for the next edition—slated to open September 3 and run through November 21—is Kulapat Yantrasast, the revered architect behind museum projects for institutions including the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Louvre, Harvard Art Museums, and the Art Institute of Chicago (as well as others while he worked for Tadao Ando).

“At a time when the world needs dialogue and understanding more than ever, culture can bring people together and open space for a shared future,” Bukhara Biennial commissioner Gayane Umerova said in a press release announcing the theme, which will be organized around four parts: Local Hospitality, Co-Creation, Resilience and Biodiversity, and Living Heritage. “For centuries, Bukhara welcomed travelers, craftspeople and merchants from across the world, and that openness shaped its identity. Through the biennial, we want to carry this legacy forward through contemporary art, so that it becomes part of life in the city, creates opportunities for its residents and leaves a lasting cultural legacy.”

Yantrasast added: “The Long Welcome celebrates the spirit of hospitality that made Bukhara worth crossing continents to reach, and worth returning to again and again. When people welcome you into their city, you want to give something back. My hope is that an artist who returns to Bukhara years from now will find that…
items.t: Bukhara Biennial Unveils ‘The Long Welcome’ Theme and Names First Artists

items.title: Iraq’s Museums Are Finally Opening Their Doors Again
items.summary:
In 2022, Iraq’s National Museum in Baghdad reopened after being closed for three years following political unrest. Then in 2024, the museum closed again, this time for renovations. Now, it’s scheduled to open on December 1.

The Art Newspaper reported that the museum will open with several new galleries, such as the Abbasid and Islamic galleries. There will also be specially curated wings. 

The museum will display artifacts including winged bulls (lamassu) and stone carvings depicting legendary Assyrian monarchs, ancient clay tablets and historical prisms recording legal codes, calligraphic friezes, stone carvings, glassworks, and mosaics that have been recovered and restored. According to the newspaper Iraqi News , the museum’s doors are opening to domestic visitors, international tourists, and researchers from around the world.

The reopening of the museum has been a long time coming. In 2003, the National Museum was the subject of looting during the US-led invasion. Ali Al-Dakhili, Iraq’s Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, has said that reopening the museum in December, rather than January 2027, is a priority, and that he also has plans for “a new building that befits the historical and civilizational value of Iraq.” 

Paul Collins, the keeper of the Middle East Department at the British Museum, told the Art Newspaper that the reopening of the museum “is an important moment, reflecting Iraq’s strong commitment to preserving its world-renowned cultural heritage and promoting heritage tourism.”

As Iraq rebuilds itself after years of political unrest, the museums’…
items.t: Iraq’s Museums Are Finally Opening Their Doors Again

items.title: EVA International Announces Theme for 50th Anniversary Edition in 2027
items.summary:
The EVA International biennial in Limerick, Ireland, will celebrate its 50th anniversary next year. Running from August 27 to October 27, it will be titled “Forms of Inheritance.”

The biennial also announced that Matt Packer will step down after 10 years as director in spring 2028. 

EVA’s organizers said in a release that the upcoming theme will question “the values between the past and the future” during a time when “promises carried forward from the late twentieth century—integration, openness and shared progress—can no longer be taken as given.” The works on view will pull from EVA International’s history with a series of new artist commissions, as well as other commissions that focus on the wider historical narratives between Ireland and Europe.

The new works at the biennale will include a work by Lisa Freeman in response to Minerva Cuevas’s Story of the Celtic Tiger , which was made for the 2006 EVA International in 2006. Dina Mimi will exhibit a work that follows the cross-generational solidarity between Irish Republican and Palestinian prisoners, while Sam Keogh’s large-scale “cartoons” installation will be based on the The Hunt of the Unicorn tapestry. To mark the biennial’s semicentennial, the 2027 program will host events and publications such as “Still (the) Barbarians?” a publication of testimonies and critical reflections of the 2016 EVA International, which will be published in early 2027 with the John Hansard Gallery.

The biennial will also change the curatorial organization of its main exhibition in which a guest curator takes on the task. Instead,…
items.t: EVA International Announces Theme for 50th Anniversary Edition in 2027

items.title: Dora Maar’s Paris Apartment Is For Sale, Picasso Wall Drawings and All
items.summary:
In this quiet, 17th-century Parisian apartment on rue de Savoie in the 6th arrondissement, strange-looking insects appear to be climbing up the middle of the living room wall near the chimney. But these 15 or so critters—spiders, ants, and cockroaches—are actually drawn and carefully protected by glass coverings. 

That’s because they were made by none other than Pablo Picasso, once a regular visitor to this home, where his lover, the artist Dora Maar, lived from 1946 until she died in 1997. The abode, along with the Picasso drawings on the wall, is now for sale, listed for the lump sum of €2.85 million (about $3.1 million), reports Le Parisien . How’s that for a dinner party icebreaker?

Small drawings of insects by Pablo Picasso have been carefully preserved on the wall of Dora Maar’s former Paris apartment. ©Agence Menager Hug 2026 

Picasso used to call Maar “ ma puce ,” which literally means “my flea” and is used as an endearing term in French for “my sweetheart.” It is believed Picasso’s drawings were a playful pun on his nickname for Maar, per the apartment’s current owner, identified only as Ida. “They give it a history,” she added.

All the wall artworks have been officially recognized by the Picasso Administration, which manages the artist’s estate, and oversees a committee that catalogs his works.

A close-up of Pablo Picasso’s insect drawings in Dora Maar’s former Paris apartment. ©Agence Menager Hug 2026. 

Many may know Maar (1907–97) as the famous figure Picasso depicted in many paintings over the course of their seven-year relationship, including his…
items.t: Dora Maar’s Paris Apartment Is For Sale, Picasso Wall Drawings and All

items.title: A Minimalist, a Maximalist, and 30 Years of Friendship
items.summary:
Two person shows are taking over the art world, with galleries doubling as matchmakers, mostly pairing dead artists with market darlings. But of course, nothing beats conversation between two old friends. 

At Gladstone in New York this fall, that’s just what you’ll get, with a new show from British artists Sarah Lucas and Cerith Wyn Evans titled “Je Pense.” 

The two talked to Art in America about the exhibition, and their 30-year friendship, below.

You two have been friends since the ’90s. How’d you meet? 

Cerith Wyn Evan s: I never can answer questions like that because I never remember. We were probably both drunk somewhere.

Sarah Lucas: It’s tricky.

CWE: I do remember hearing of you. I was close with a painter at the time, Angus Cook, and I’d ask him things like “What’s Gary Hume like?,” all this kind of stuff. Later I quipped, “We should really be talking about his girlfriend , a much better artist. She’s called Sarah Lucas.”

Angus said he had met you once: He knocked on the door and you answered—allegedly!—and he said “Hi, are you Gary?” and you replied “NO.” He told me “Oh my God, She’s incredible!”

SL: I remember meeting Angus at a party Matthew Marks gave for Gary, maybe that’s where I met you. A lot of things were happening at that time, around 1990; something was burgeoning. I met a lot of people then that became friends for life.

CWE: There was a mileuuuu. 

You can’t make new old friends! When I saw that you two were showing together, I admit my first thought was: a minimalist and a maximalist walk into a bar. 

CWE: Who’s who? [laughs] I’m certainly…
items.t: A Minimalist, a Maximalist, and 30 Years of Friendship

items.title: The Royal Court’s new mission? To boldly go back to the 60s space race with The Afronauts
items.summary:
Royal Court theatre, London
Ryan Calais Cameron’s ‘true(ish)’ account of a charismatic freedom fighter’s plan to take a Zambian crew to the moon never quite lifts off

Ryan Calais Cameron has proved himself a playwright of stratospheric talent. His previous plays For Black Boys Who Have Considered Suicide When the Hue Gets Too Heavy and Retrograde both streaked their way into the West End. This new one is filled with mighty ambition but does not lift off in the same way.

It is based on what he calls a “true(ish)” story. The figure of Edward Mukuka Nkoloso (Lucian Msamati) is taken from Zambian history. A freedom fighter for the nation’s independence in the 1960s, he set up a national academy for science and trained a group of “afronauts” in the hope of beating the US and the Soviet Union in the race to reach the moon. Nkoloso, a kind of Dead Poets Society inspiration figure here, picks 17-year-old Martha (Ama Qamata) for the mission.

items.title: Frieze Los Angeles Lines Up 102 Exhibitors for 2027 Edition
items.summary:
Frieze Los Angeles has named the 102 exhibitors that will participate in its upcoming 2027 edition, scheduled to run February 25–28 at the Santa Monica Airport.

The line-up includes several returning blue-chip galleries like Gagosian, Hauser & Wirth, Pace Gallery, David Zwirner, White Cube, Lisson, Gladstone, Sprüth Magers, and Thaddaeus Ropac. Galleries returning to the fair after an absence include Regen Projects, Luis De Jesus Los Angeles, Mariane Ibrahim, and Petzel.

Though several LA-based galleries and LA outposts for larger galleries have closed in the past year and a half, Frieze LA will feature 38 exhibitors with spaces in the City of Angels. They include Commonwealth and Council, Vielmetter, Marc Selwyn Fine Art, Charlie James, Night Gallery, Parker Gallery, Roberts Projects, and Make Room, which has been promoted to the main Galleries section.

“Los Angeles has many centers, each with its own history and communities, and you feel that in the work artists make here: the personal histories they draw on and the questions they’re asking about belonging and who public space is for,” Frieze Americas director Christine Messineo said in a statement. “For the city’s galleries, this is their hometown fair, a moment for the whole LA art world to show the work being made now, by artists across generations. What I love is that visitors from around the world get to experience this work right where it comes from.”

The fair will feature 22 first-time exhibitors, with 10 of them coming from the Focus section, for emerging galleries, which will be organized by Hammer curator…
items.t: Frieze Los Angeles Lines Up 102 Exhibitors for 2027 Edition

items.title: A New Museum in Georgia’s Wine Country Shows Another Side of the Country’s Art History
items.summary:
A long journey from Tokyo to the island of Naoshima to see art gave Jemal Inaishvili, a shipping executive and collector, an idea for how he might convince people to make a similar trek within his home country of Georgia in the South Caucasus. Unlike visiting Naoshima, which typically involves a full day of travel, the drive from the capital city of Tbilisi to Kakheti, Georgia’s eastern wine region, is around two hours, three in heavy traffic. “Of course, I cannot copy them,” he told me recently, “but I will do something similar, but based on Georgian art.”

The result is the Kvareli Foundation for Contemporary Art, which opened to the public earlier this month on land Inaishvili bought a decade ago for a small winery. The site now also holds a hotel, a sculpture park, and a red-slatted museum with a rooftop for performances and film screenings by the Tbilisi practice Midamo. This admission-free venue will stage four exhibitions a year, drawing from Inaishvili’s collection of about 1,000 works.

To lead the programming, Inaishvili has hired 28-year-old Nino Sulkhanishvili. “Sometimes one’s experience will be the barrier,” he said of the creative director, who is in her first institutional role. “Together with the foundation, she is also growing.”

In heading up a private museum, Sulkhanishvili sees her role as helping to give Georgian artists the infrastructure to exhibit at home, like Elene Chantladze, whose solo show will open at the Kvareli Foundation in February. Such a setting, Sulkhanishvili said, “is extremely important, especially in your own country. … I feel…

items.title: Simon Brodkin: ‘Which of my pranks went badly wrong? Well, Boris Johnson became PM after the Theresa May one’
items.summary:
The character comedian AKA Lee Nelson handed May a P45 and threw golf balls at Donald Trump. He explains why the pranking’s now on ice – and which funny footballers inspired him

How did you get into comedy?
I was booted out of every class for making jokes and then I discovered, at medical school, there is such a thing as a career in comedy. I was encouraged by being able to entertain the patients and went straight from that into comedy.

Who did you admire when you were starting out?
It was always the character comedians: Sacha Baron Cohen, Ricky Gervais, Steve Coogan. On the circuit Al Murray was doing the Pub Landlord. I admired anyone doing characters who could be dropped into multiple situations. As I started doing character comedy myself, I was inspired by people who might not have known how funny they were, such as a big batch of Premier League footballers from Beckham to Gerrard to Rooney.

Simon Brodkin: Unleashed is at the Apollo, London, on 13 December and 11 March and on tour in the UK until 26 May

items.title: Dylan Moran goes looking for trouble and disappears off the beaten track in this baffling comedy show
items.summary:
Royal & Derngate, Northampton
The Black Books star gets off to a promising start as he contemplates ‘the burning ball of what you don’t understand’ but his search for levity leads to half-baked ditties

Is Dylan Moran joking when he opens his show by telling Northampton’s audience “I didn’t write anything, or prepare”? By the end, you wouldn’t bet on it. Bleary directionlessness may be par for the course for the Irish comic, whose work has always combined poetic-philosophical dazzle with a certain wooziness. But after a promising start tonight, his new touring show, Looking for Trouble, conspicuously loses its way, as Moran frets about forgetting a significant chunk of material, before abandoning his encore and leaving a bewildered audience in his wake.

That’s a shame, because there are shards of trademark brilliance in the opening 20 minutes, which see the 55-year-old address himself, albeit obliquely, to the mysteries of being human in 2026, AKA “the burning ball of what you don’t understand” From Trump to AI, Moran surveys it all in wide angle not closeup, as symptoms of our confusion, atavism and fear of expulsion from the tribe. The quality of his thinking in this section, while cheerfully offering himself up as Exhibit A in this prosecution of humanity’s perplexity, is arresting. And there are zingers, too, including a word-picture of the genitals that, once heard, may never be forgotten.
items.t: Dylan Moran goes looking for trouble and disappears off the beaten track in this baffling comedy show

items.title: Nine Night is back and proves itself a modern classic full of secrets, squabbles and laughs
items.summary:
Kiln theatre, London
Exquisitely acted, and directed with lightness and depth, Natasha Gordon’s 2018 tragicomedy about a Jamaican matriarch’s wake is moving and never mawkish

The death of a parent has a way of blowing up the lives of family members it leaves behind. The combustions of grief, greed and secrets revealed around a barely buried coffin litter the tragicomic works of playwrights such as Tracy Letts (August: Osage County) and Branden Jacobs-Jenkins (Appropriate).

You might want to add Natasha Gordon’s debut play to that canon, although it comes wrapped in its own distinct cultural tradition. Its structure revolves around the Caribbean funeral ritual that commemorates the death of a loved one over nine nights. A debut play written by a young Black British woman, featuring an almost entirely Black British cast, it got a huge reaction at the National Theatre in 2018.

Continue reading...

items.title: Lend them your ears! Julius Caesar is staged with just four actors – and a great big gong
items.summary:
Sam Wanamaker Playhouse, London
This truncated, candlelit version makes use of skilful percussion to occasionally fill in for oration but loses some of the play’s beauty and power

Any modern reformulation of Julius Caesar may inevitably be compared with Phyllida Lloyd’s innovative, all-female 2012 production, now revived by the Royal Shakespeare Company, which reimagined the tragedy as a play-within-a-play in a women’s prison.

This reworked version, adapted and directed by Joe Hill-Gibbins, does not match its depth and originality but certainly does something different. It is performed at 90 minutes straight-through with just four actors who take on the central roles of conspirators Cassius (Natey Jones) and Brutus (Caoilfhionn Dunne) alongside Mark Antony (Adam Gillen) and Caesar (Kate Duchêne, who also plays the soothsayer and Octavius). It is not as gimmicky as you may think.

items.summary:
Norwich Theatre Royal
Magic is sprinkled over Michael Pink’s elegant show, with the spirited score played by the Northern Ballet Sinfonia

It wouldn’t be the first time an ugly sister has stolen the show. Andrew Tomlinson is a hoot in Northern Ballet’s new Cinderella as a klutzy, vainglorious stepsister with a great line in lovably grotesque facial expressions. He certainly provides some panto-like festivity in the midst of an otherwise very nice ballet.

Getting its UK premiere, this pretty Cinderella is choreographed by Michael Pink, who was associate artistic director at Northern Ballet in the 1990s, and it feels very much like the Northern Ballet of old: accessible and enjoyable mainstream dance with clear storytelling. (It was originally made for Milwaukee Ballet, where Pink has been artistic director since 2002.)

items.title: Ben Whishaw and Kathryn Hunter are a dynamite duo on the road to nowhere in Eurotrash
items.summary:
Young Vic, London
Adaptation of Christian Kracht’s novel is full of heartwarming comedy as a mother and son take a trip to distribute ‘dirty money’ to good causes

You would be hard-pushed to find a more charismatic double act than Kathryn Hunter and Ben Whishaw. She dazzles as a dowager, bringing flamboyant physical flourishes as she knocks back the cooking wine; he is her lugubrious son, Christian, a novelist with writer’s block. Their story trades on kookiness but the chemistry would keep you captivated even if they watched paint dry for the duration of this interval-free drama.

Based on Swiss author Christian Kracht’s bestselling novel, adapted by Colin Teevan, it is charmingly directed by Walter Meierjohann. The third big star is Lizzie Clachan’s set, so full of mischief that it is like a magician pulling out imaginative visual jokes and clever thrills and spills. Glyn Pritchard heroically plays ancillary roles (from taxi driver to waiter) with lightning-quick wardrobe changes while the sound effects are visibly, wittily created in a glass studio.

items.title: Can depression really become dazzling dance? The biggest ever BalletBoyz show is a huge feat
items.summary:
Sadler’s Wells, London
In Six Lethargies, Iván Pérez and Seirian Griffiths have devised a mammoth production of aching, ethereal sadness

‘If I write what I feel, will you feel it, too?” That was the question behind singer-songwriter turned composer Keaton Henson’s Six Lethargies. Perhaps that is every artist’s mission, but for Henson it was specifically his experiences with anxiety and depression that he wanted to translate into music. Now it has been turned into dance by the BalletBoyz. If they dance it, will we feel it?

Six Lethargies is the largest production in the 25-year history of the BalletBoyz. Once just two ex-Royal Ballet dancers, Michael Nunn and William Trevitt, this iteration is a company of 44 dancers (male and female), a 37-piece string orchestra, and not one but two choreographers working together: former Dance Theatre Heidelberg artistic director Iván Pérez and talented newcomer Seirian Griffiths.

items.title: Pink Rabbit: the provocative bedroom drama about a Muslim OnlyFans star interrupted by her mum
items.summary:
In Farah Ashraf’s solo show an obedient daughter secretly does online sex work as ‘PersianBaby’. The actor and writer explains how two worlds collide in her darkly funny play

At home, Amna is the modest and dutiful Muslim daughter of her parents’ dreams. Online, armed with a webcam and an OnlyFans account, she is PersianBaby – an exoticised version of herself complete with fake accent, designed to entice men willing to part with their cash.

Pink Rabbit, writer-performer Farah Ashraf’s provocative and darkly funny solo play, is a nuanced account of being caught between the private life of desire and the cultural expectations that shape how she is perceived. “I loved this idea of push and pull, and two different worlds,” says Ashraf who began work on the play during her final year at the Oxford School of Drama, before which she had trained with the National Youth Theatre.
